23119-a-forgotten-hero-or-not-for-him:
Clarice dresses with care in A Forgotten Hero, or Not for Him. Clarice wears her dark hair brushed smooth and curled up all around, cut short enough for the style. Her gown is long and loose in the Princess fashion, its train tucked under one arm as she walks.

Fashion detail like this carries the social world of the tale, where a forgotten hero's worth must be weighed against appearances. The double title poses the heroine's question, is the overlooked man for her, or not? Domestic fiction of the period loved that weighing. Dress, visits, and small slights build the scales. Readers get a quiet courtship problem, dressed in Princess style and judged by character in the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abarim: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Abarim describes a mountain range across the Jordan, running south from Mount Nebo, perhaps reaching the Arabian desert. The Vulgate gives its meaning as passages. Its north end bore the name Phasga, or Pisgah, whose highest peak was Mount Nebo. Balaam blessed Israel a second time from Mount Phasga, Moses saw the Land of Promise from there, and Jeremias hid the ark there, according to the Second Book of Maccabees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-von-be:
Albert von Behaim, also known as Albertus Bohemus, was a papal partisan in the struggle with the Emperor Frederick II, born about 1180 near Passau and dead there in 1260. He went to Rome in 1205 and served at the papal court as a legal expert. In 1237 he returned to Germany and helped form a league against Frederick between the rulers of Bavaria, Bohemia, and Austria.

When Frederick was excommunicated in 1239, Behaim became permanent papal delegate. He pressed the sentence on Germany's bishops, excommunicating negligent clergy and laymen of rank when they failed him. His severity bore no fruit, and he had to leave the country, though he kept working against the emperor at the Council of Lyons in 1245. He ended his days at Passau, where he had been dean of the chapter since 1246, leaving two diaries known as the Missivbücher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-joseph-:
Anton Joseph Binterim, a German theologian born at Dusseldorf in 1779, served fifty years as parish priest of Bilk. After Franciscan training, he was ordained at Cologne in 1802, then left religious life when his monastery was suppressed. Appointed pastor of Bilk in 1805, he stayed until his death in 1855, writing tirelessly in defence of the church.

His treatises answered the rationalists of his day from ancient church and literary sources. He also fought Prussian law on mixed marriages, which stripped mothers of rights over their children's faith. Enemies accused him of intrigue with Rome, and he spent six months jailed at Wesel. The entry presents a combative pastor-scholar who never left his parish post.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-pannar:
Arnold Pannartz and Konrad Sweinheim, both printers, Pannartz dead about 1476 and Sweinheim in 1477, brought Gutenberg's invention to Italy. Pannartz was perhaps from Prague and Sweinheim from Eltville near Mainz, where Zedler believes Sweinheim worked with Gutenberg in 1461 to 1464. Whether Pannartz had joined Sweinheim in Germany is unknown, but together they carried printing south.

The Benedictine monastery of Subiaco became the cradle of Italian printing, probably at the summons of Cardinal Giovanni of Turrecremata, its commendatory abbot. They arrived in 1464, and their first Subiaco book, a Donatus grammar, has not survived. The first Italian printed book still extant is their Cicero, On the Orator, issued in September 1465, followed by Lactantius in October 1465 and Augustine's City of God in 1467.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baal-baalim:
Baal, plural Baalim, is a Semitic word meaning lord or owner. In Hebrew a man is called baal of a house, a field, cattle, wealth, and a wife. A ram is baal of two horns, and Joseph's brothers called him a baal of dreams. Inscriptions show the same broad use in other Semitic tongues. In the Hebrew Bible the plural keeps the singular's senses, though translations use it only for deities. The local Baals named are gods, not images.

As a god's name, Baal kept its sense of ownership and was qualified: Baal of Tyre, Harran, Tarsus, Hermon, Lebanon, Tamar, and heaven. Several Baals held titles, among them Baal of the Covenant in Judges. The article goes on to trace Baal worship, its emblems, and its place in Israel's religion. It draws on a source list from Movers to Smend. Its notes guide on the plural in Samuel and Kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cherubim:
An entry on the cherubim, angelic beings or their images, named often in the Old Testament and a single time in the New. The word cherub comes from the Assyrian kirubu, from a root meaning to be near, so cherubim are the near ones, the courtiers who surround God's majesty. The entry notes the word should be spoken qerub, with a hard sound.

In art, cherubim most often mean the sculpted, engraved, and embroidered figures that adorned the Jewish sanctuary. Two gold figures stood on the lid of the Ark, and Solomon set two huge olive-wood figures overlaid with gold in the Holy of Holies. Cherubim were also embroidered on the veil between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies and engraved as a motif, a repeated design, in wood and metal through the Temple. The entry weighs their forms and their place in worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dietrich-von-:
Dietrich von Nieheim, a German historian of the Middle Ages, was born between 1338 and 1340 in Paderborn's diocese. He took his name from the small town of Nieheim and spent years studying law in Italy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him into the papal chancery at Avignon under Urban the Fifth, where he served as a notary. He went with Gregory the Eleventh back to Rome in 1377.

Dietrich is best known for his writings on the Western Schism, the split that set rival popes against each other. As abbreviator and later servant of the curia, he watched the crisis from inside. He died at Maastricht in 1418, leaving chronicles that historians still use to trace the schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elohim:
Elohim is the common Hebrew name for God. This entry weighs its form, its sense, and its roots. It is a plural form. Yet the usage of the language gives no support, the entry insists, to the idea that it preserves early polytheism or a blend with higher spirits. Grammarians call it a plural of majesty, rank, abstraction, or magnitude. The Ethiopic plural amlak likewise became a proper name for God.

Etymology divides scholars. Some take Elohim as the plural of Eloah, from a root meaning dread or seeking refuge. The name then first meant the object of dread. Others take it from El, with Eloah grown from a stem meaning mighty. The entry notes that forty-one of the fifty-seven uses of Eloah fall in Job. The rest fall in late or poetic texts. It tests each theory against the texts with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-gom:
Francisco Gomes de Amorim, born at Avelomar near Oporto on 13 August 1827 and dead on 4 November 1891, was a Portuguese poet, dramatist, and novelist of the Romantic age. His parents were respectable yet so poor that he left school at ten, went to Brazil, and worked in a business house at Para. There he studied the manners and dialects of Amazon Indian tribes. Returning to Portugal at twenty, he came under the spell of Almeida Garrett and the plan for a national drama.

Under the revolutionary ideas of 1848 he wrote poems on liberty, the fall of Hungary, and Garibaldi. His first play, Ghigi, performed at Lisbon in 1852 with signal success, began a long series of dramas, including Odio de raca, Aleijoes sociaes, Figados de tigre. A prohibicao, A viuva, A abnegacao, and Os herdeiros do millionario followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-jose:
Francois Joseph Heim, born near Belfort in 1787 and dead at Paris in 1865, was a French historical painter of early talent and long official honour. He began work at eight and won first prize for drawing at Strasburg before eleven. In 1803 his family sent him to Paris to study under Vincent, the best teaching they could afford. In 1807 he won an Academy prize with Theseus and the Minotaur and a travelling scholarship that took him to Rome.

Back in Paris he won the Academy's gold medal, became a full member in 1829 and professor in 1831. He was appointed painter to the Institute of France, exhibiting over sixty portraits of members whose drawings now hang in the Louvre. His historical and religious pictures were very attractive, the best being Jacob in Mesopotamia, painted in 1814 and now at Bordeaux.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-corn:
Renaissance figure Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim, born at Cologne in 1486, was by reputation knight, doctor, and magician, and he earned and repaid his conservative enemies' hatred across a wandering life. Student at Cologne and Paris, teacher of Hebrew at Dôle and in England, soldier under Maximilian who knighted him, he finished his Occult Philosophy, a blend of Neoplatonism and Cabala, about 1510.

Banished from Cologne for debt and dying poor at Grenoble or Lyons in 1534 or 1535, he left works steeped in occultism. They attacked scholasticism, relic veneration, canon law, and hierarchy while calling Scripture the philosopher's stone. Openly sympathetic to Luther's tone without joining him, he influenced Giordano Bruno. His 1527 book on the vanity of the sciences was translated across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hildesheim:
Hildesheim is a German diocese in Hanover east of the Weser, plus the duchy of Brunswick, founded under Emperor Louis the Pious. Legend says a miracle moved Louis to choose the present cathedral site over the village of Elze, where he built Germany's first chapel dedicated to the Mother of God. The founding date varies by account from 814 to 822, and the first bishop was Gunthar.

Rich gifts, immunities, and feudal sovereignty soon brought the see prosperity and power. Its brightest age came under Bishops Bernward, Godehard, and Hezilo in the eleventh century. Bernward's taste gave the cathedral its famous bronze doors, the Christ column, and the Bernward cross, plus the church of St. Michael, whose western crypt holds his tomb. Gandersheim Abbey also belonged to its orbit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-nico:
Johannes Nicolaus von Hontheim, writing as Justinus Febronius, was an auxiliary bishop of Trier whose book on the Church's constitution stirred a famous controversy. Born at Trier in 1701, he studied law and theology at Trier, Louvain, and Leyden, where the Gallican doctrines of Van Espen shaped him. Ordained in 1728, he became professor of the Pandects at Trier, then dean of St. Simeon, auxiliary bishop, and vicar-general.

In 1763 he published his treatise on the state of the Church and the lawful power of the Roman pontiff, arguing for limits on papal authority that became known as Febronianism. The book drew condemnation and long debate across Germany. Only two years before his death in 1790 did he renounce his doctrines with full sincerity. The entry paints him as short, energetic, hard-working, pious, and generous, yet faulted for spreading Gallican ideas in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-and-mich:
John Banim was an Irish poet, dramatist, and novelist whose work with his brother Michael aimed to do for Ireland what Scott had done for Scotland. Born at Kilkenny in 1798, he wrote verses and a tale by age ten, studied art at Dublin, and taught drawing on his return. A refused love ended in the girl's death and his own paralysis, leaving him a victim of spinal disease for life.

At twenty-three his tragedy Damon and Pythias staged at Covent Garden, Macready and Charles Kemble in the cast. With Michael he planned the Tales of the O'Hara Family, each brother revising the other's work so closely that their shares cannot be told apart. Moving to London in 1822, he poured out dramas, essays, and novels through constant pain, painting Irish character, brightly lit and deeply shadowed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-sweynh: This 1913 reference piece on Sweynheim — the Subiaco printer. Heinrich Wallau honors his famous press. His types gave Italy the classics. The age prized the printed page. The libraries keep his name. His 1477 death is famed. His 1465 press is famed. His 1465 Italian classics are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-langheim: A 1913 entry on Langheim — the Franconian abbey. Edmond Obrecht gives its storied past. Its monks guard the ancient church. The ages bless the holy house. The Main guards its walls. Its 1132 founding is famed. Its monks are famed. Its 1132 Cistercian house is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-behaim: A 1913 entry on Behaim — the Nuremberg navigator. Otto Hartig honors his famous globe. His art mapped the unknown seas. Germany hailed the daring name. The fifteenth century knew his fame. His 1507 death is famed. His 1492 globe is famed. His 1492 Erdapfel globe is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-cu: A 1913 entry on the Cuncolim Martyrs — the Goan victims. Anthony D'Souza unfolds their fateful tale. They sealed the faith with blood. The order bless the holy names. The sixteenth century knew their deaths. Their 1583 deaths are famed. Their 1583 martyrdoms are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micheas-of-ep: A 1913 entry on Micheas of Ephraim — the minor prophet. Albin Van Hoonacker unfolds his oracles. He warned the idolatrous tribes. The Book keeps the hallowed words. The ages bless his name. Its 1907 study is famed. His prophetic words are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-midrashim: This 1913 reference piece on the Midrashim — the rabbinic lore. Francis Gigot unfolds their exegetic art. They unfold the sacred text. The scholars prize the seemly tomes. The rabbis keep their form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its homiletic art is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naim: At Nain, Jesus met a widow's funeral procession and raised her only son, moved by her tears. This entry covers the Gospel story, the town's site, and its church. Compassion that conquered death: the Church built its shrine over the miracle's site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piligrim: Piligrim was the bishop of Passau who evangelized the Hungarians in the 900s. This entry covers his career, his missions, and the forgeries ascribed to him. The apostle of the Hungarian frontier: his ancient Passau became a great missionary see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purim: Purim is the Jewish feast of Esther's deliverance. This entry explains its origin, its observance, and its meaning. The festival of the lots: its joyful megillah tells the Esther story in synagogue each spring in Adar's bright joy and noise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-of-rud: Rudolf of Rüdesheim was the bishop-diplomat of Lavant. This entry notes his embassies, his episcopate, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A churchman of the conciliar age: his papal missions served the council of Basel in the 1430s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seraphim: The seraphim are the burning ones of Isaias. This entry examines their name, their office, and their choir. The highest of the angelic hosts: their six wings veil the throne in Isaias' vision in the Temple of Jerusalem in the Holy of Holies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joachim: St. Joachim was the father of the Virgin Mary. This entry traces his Anna, his temple, and his cult. The patriarch of the holy family: his ancient feast crowned the Church in the calendar of the year in the liturgy.
doe-osti-2996974-modeling-detonation-wit: Blast waves got their computer twin, and this DOE report runs the CartaBlanca sims. The pages detail the detonation runs. The weapons scientists get their tool. The twin was CartaBlanca. The runs were detonation. The tool was weapons. The sims were detonation.

doe-osti-3452149-the-radioisotope-power-: RPS-DET got manual-versioned, and this DOE user covers dose estimation tools. The pages detail the radioisotope findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The version was 2.0. The data were nuclear. The RPS-DET were manual. The tool were estimation.
george-leatrim:
George Leatrim, or The Mother's Test, by Susanna Moodie, opens as a story told between friends. One lady calls it the most terrible instance of dishonesty she ever knew, in her own family's branches. Dr Leatrim, the subject, preaches at Westcliff. He is eloquent in the pulpit and solitary out of it. Some great domestic calamity, people say, weaned him from the world. Since his wife and only son died, no one has seen him smile.

Benevolence breathes from his sermons, his friend protests, from so austere a man. Moodie, the Canadian pioneer author of Roughing It in the Bush, wrote this tale of an English clergyman's hidden wound. The mother's test of the subtitle is the story's engine. A reputation for austere goodness is the mask. Behind it sits a theft, a sacrifice, and a mother's terrible arithmetic of love.
gerhard-the-coming-creed-of-the-world-is: The Coming Creed of the World, is there not a faith more sublime, by Gerhard. The future faith. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BishopJim_Bisho:
Jim Bishop was the journalist who turned single days into bestsellers: The Day Lincoln Was Shot, The Day Christ Died, and The Day Kennedy Was Shot. This magazine profile looks at the man behind that formula.

Bishop rebuilt famous days hour by hour from documents and interviews, and readers bought his books by the million. His Kennedy volume appeared in 1968 and carried his method to the assassination that defines this archive. A profile in a researcher's files shows the attention paid to the popular historians who shaped how America pictured November 22, 1963.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAJim_CIA_Jim:
A man identified only as 'Jim,' a former CIA contract agent, told a radio interviewer that the CIA was responsible for a massacre in the Congo. United Press International carried the report, drawn from his interview with Art Kevin of station KMPC.

Such claims surfaced through the 1960s and 1970s, as contract men from the Congo wars talked to journalists and the agency declined to answer. A wire report is the thinnest form of the story: the claim, the claimant's first name, and no adjudication. It is preserved as it moved on the wire, a fragment of the Congo's long and contested record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HoughtonJim_Hou: Harold Weisberg wrote on November 27, 2004 to Tony Marro of Newsday about Jim Hougan's book Secret Agenda. Weisberg, then in his nineties, was still arguing the cases of his life in letters to journalists. The surviving record gives the date, the recipient, and the book under discussion, but not the letter's arguments, so it stands as very late Weisberg correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McNicholasJim_M: nsia-McNicholasJim McNicholas Jim: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TurnerJim_Turne: FBI agents interviewed Jim Turner, television director at WBAP-TV in Fort Worth, on July 22, 1964. The subject was his station's coverage of Lee Harvey Oswald's transfer, the event during which Jack Ruby shot Oswald on live television. Broadcasters were witnesses as well as reporters that weekend. The interview records what a man who helped put those pictures on air told the bureau.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Al:
Allende and Chile: Bring Him Down appeared in November 2020, days after the fiftieth anniversary of Salvador Allende's history-changing election as president of Chile. Its title quotes the spirit of Washington's orders toward his elected government.

The briefing book publishes records of the American campaign against Allende: money for opponents, propaganda, and economic pressure meant to make Chile's economy scream, as President Nixon put it. Released half a century on, the documents still carry force, because the campaign worked and a coup followed in 1973. For readers of that coup, the collection supplies the prequel in the plotters' own files.
jimgrim:
Jimgrim is an adventure novel by Talbot Mundy, published in 1922. Its contents page shows a long tale in two parts and twenty chapters. Part one is called The Reincarnated. Part two is called Messiah of Tinsel. Chapter titles speak in riddles and half-quoted lines. One offers to take a case, and another toys with crowning Jimgrim emperor.

Several chapters turn on a figure named Dorje, styled the Daring and the King of the World. One chapter asks for the key to Dorje's cipher, and another prints a long string of numbers. A woman claims to be the Queen of Sheba and says Jimgrim's name was stolen. Mundy's chapter list promises secret identities, codes, and intrigue around his hero Jimgrim.
markheim:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this short tale of a murder on Christmas Day, and it came out in 1885. It was first bound in his set The Merry Men, from which this text is drawn. Stevenson had a rare gift for the dark side of the soul in a brief tale.

Markheim, a dealer in old goods, kills a shop man for cash on the holy day. A strange guest then steps in, who may be the devil, or the man's own soul made plain. The talk that comes next probes guilt and grace with a force few short tales match.
more-goops-and-how-not-to-be-them-a-manu:
Gelett Burgess wrote this manual of manners for impolite infants as a sequel to his Goops book. Frederick A. Stokes published it at New York with ninety illustrations by the author. The Goops are naughty, thoughtless children shown in comic verse. Each picture and rhyme displays a fault for young readers to avoid.

Burgess, a San Francisco humorist, first made the Goops famous in magazines. The catalog pages list his nonsense books and lively city fairy tales. Parents bought the Goops books to teach table manners, cleanliness, and kindness by laughter. The sequel's subtitle promises the characteristics of many naughty children, depicted so that polite infants will not copy them.
nasa-tm-19660018727-irradiation-system-f:
F A Haley and R R Wyer at Lewis Research Center described an irradiation system for very cold experiments. The system works inside the Plum Brook Reactor. Their paper was prepared for a May 1966 meeting in California. Cryogenic work studies matter at extremely low temperatures. Doing it inside a reactor adds radiation to the cold. Their system lets samples sit in both conditions at once, under control.

Such combined tests serve reactor and space research alike. Materials in space face cold and radiation together, not one at a time. A purpose-built system makes the pair testable on the ground. The paper was offered for a symposium on irradiation capsule technology, where specialists traded designs for exactly this kind of rig.
nasa-tm-19720002890-target-contrast-cons:
A Mayer of the Ames Research Center wrote this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,082. It sets target signal needs for aircraft navigation systems that see by heat radiation. A radiometric receiver maps the faint power radiated by terrain below. It can also map beacons placed on the ground. Either map could guide an aircraft in poor visibility.

Mayer focused on waves near eight millimeters long. At chosen bands, such waves cross the air with little loss, even in extreme weather. Hardware for that size was available and compact. The small wavelength also promised sharp images. Those traits made all weather navigation by radiometry look practical.
nasa-tm-19720004689-thermal-coefficients:
Robert F. Mueller of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in October 1971, numbered X-644-71-418, on how fast nature absorbs the effects of technology. Recovery processes set that pace: plants regrowing, soil rebuilding, and pollution being cleansed from land and water. Mueller estimated thermal coefficients, heat-based rates, for these assimilation processes.

His estimates indicate that such processes run far more slowly in Earth's cold regions than in temperate ones. The difference runs from ten times to several hundred times. Cold-region environments are fragile largely because temperature limits the biological activity that repairs damage. The processes include vegetation growth, soil humus formation, and the work of microorganisms, plus chemical decay of wastes. Mueller suggests these uneven rates are important data when planning technological expansion in Arctic regions.
nasa-tm-19720005298-analysis-of-heat-tra:
Herbert J Gladden, Daniel J Gauntner, and John N B Livingood of the Lewis Research Center analyzed these vane cooling tests in December 1971, as NASA TM X-2376. The test piece was a turbine vane cooled three ways at once. Jets struck its inner wall, air scrubbed its passages, and a film of air coated its outer skin. The vane sat in a still cascade of similar blades for the tests.

Gas in the cascade reached very high heat and pressure. The catalog record gives peak values near twenty five hundred degrees Fahrenheit. The team gathered flow and heat transfer data throughout the runs. Average and local metal temperatures were matched in several ways. Turbine designers used such results to keep blades alive.
nasa-tm-19720010255-application-of-the-s:
Bobby G Junkin of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on December 10, 1971, as NASA TM X-64636. He worked in the Computation Laboratory there. The report applies the steepest ascent method to a reentry trajectory problem. Steepest ascent is a step by step way to improve a flight path. Each step nudges the controls toward the best payoff while respecting limits.

Junkin presents the direct optimization method in full detail. Starting control values enter as inputs to the process. Small test changes are then made to those controls. The method predicts, to first order, how payoff and constraint values will shift. Designers can then choose the most promising change. The approach served trajectory planning for returning spacecraft.
piccadilly-jim:
P. G. Wodehouse opens Piccadilly Jim at the Riverside Drive mansion of Mr. Peter Pett, financier. The house, he says, jumps out and bites at you, resembling in equal proportions a cathedral, a suburban villa, a hotel, and a Chinese pagoda. Mr. Pett wanders it like a lost spirit, hunting a quiet spot for his Sunday paper.

Since his marriage two years before, the place has filled with intruders, for Mrs. Pett writes voluminously and loves to be noticed. The novel's hero is her stepson Jim Crocker, the wild Piccadilly Jim of the title. Wodehouse builds farce from money, family, and mistaken identity on two continents.
robert-browning-how-to-know-him:
William Lyon Phelps, Lampson Professor of English Literature at Yale, wrote this guide to Robert Browning, with a portrait of the poet. He dedicates it to James Whitcomb Riley with sincere affection and respect. Seven chapters form the plan, from The Man to Browning's Optimism.

Chapters between treat Browning's theory of poetry, his lyrics, and his dramatic lyrics in turn. The dramatic monologues, his most famed form, get a chapter of their own. Poems of Paradox follows, asking how his strange tales serve his faith in life. A list of poems at the front runs from Abt Vogler and Andrea del Sarto to The Bishop Orders His Tomb.
robert-burns-how-to-know-him:
William Allan Neilson, professor of English at Harvard University, wrote this guide to Robert Burns, issued by Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis with copyright of 1917. A portrait by Nasmyth fronts the book, and Neilson dedicates it to his brother. He had also written Essentials of Poetry.

A list of poems with their page numbers shows the book's method: to know Burns through the poems themselves. Address to the Deil and Address to the Unco Guid stand among the first entries. Ae Fond Kiss, Afton Water, and Auld Lang Syne follow, with The Auld Farmer's New-Year Morning Salutation and The Bard's Epitaph. Songs and satires alike are set out for study.
sundown-slim:
Henry Herbert Knibbs wrote Sundown Slim, copyrighted in 1915 and printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with illustrations by Anton Fischer. The western novel is dedicated to Everett E. Haraszthy, and its chapters stay in Arizona country throughout.

The contents open with Sundown in Antelope, run through The Joke and Thirty Miles to the Concho, and follow the canon trail to a place called The Last Chance. Later chapters bring a storm, a gift, and Sundown working as a vaquero. Knibbs was a poet of the range as well as a novelist. He writes of a wandering cowboy here. The man's soft heart and tall frame carry him far. He moves through scrapes, friendships, and range work under desert skies.
t-de-witt-talmage-as-i-knew-him:
T. De Witt Talmage As I Knew Him, printed at New York by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1912, is the famous preacher's own account of his life, finished after his death with concluding chapters by Mrs. T. De Witt Talmage. The contents mark the life off in seventeen milestones, with a biographical sketch of his last milestones added.

The illustrations show Talmage's parents, David and Catherine Talmage. They show his first church at Belleville, New Jersey. They show his service as chaplain of the Thirteenth Regiment of New York. They show the third Brooklyn Tabernacle too. That was the great church he filled for years. Talmage was among the most widely read sermon writers of his century, and the book tells his rise in his own hearty, anecdotal voice.
the-dozen-from-lakerim:
Rupert Hughes's The Dozen from Lakerim, dated 1899, tells of life at a boys' academy. Hughes notes that about half ran first in St. Nicholas magazine, and begs pardon for slighting books and studies in favour of games and pranks between classes. The book is set in memory of his father, and pictures by C. M. Relyea fill its list of plates.

Twelve schoolmates, the Lakerim club, fill the tales with sport and scrapes. Scenes name a cross-country run, a boxing match, and boys tied in sacks. Hughes writes school life as play first.
the-honorable-peter-stirling-and-what-pe: Paul Leicester Ford wrote The Honorable Peter Stirling and What People Thought of Him, dated 1894, with Stitt Publishing Company and Henry Holt & Co. named on the title page. A table of contents lists thirty-three chapters, numbered in Roman numerals with no titles given for any of them. Only the title page and contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear, and no plot beyond the title's promise can be stated from what is shown.
the-passionate-pilgrim:
William Shakespeare's The Passionate Pilgrim is a group of poems on love, printed here under numbered headings. The first poem begins with a lover whose mistress swears she is made of truth. He says he believes her, though he knows she lies, so that she may think him a simple youth. Both hide their age, since love's best habit is a soothing tongue.

The second poem speaks of two loves, one of comfort and one of despair. A fair man is the poet's better angel, and a dark woman his worser spirit, who tempts the angel from his side. The third poem turns to a woman's eye and a broken vow. Doubt and jealousy run through the set.
the-talleyrand-maxim: J. S. Fletcher's Talleyrand Maxim is dated 1920, and this record gives its title page and chapter list without any of the novel itself. Seventeen chapters are named, starting with Death Brings Opportunity and moving through In Trust, The Shop-Boy, The Fortunate Possessors, and Point-Blank. Later headings mention a power of attorney, a first trick, and cards laid on the table. The skeleton suggests a mystery of money, trust, and scheming, though Fletcher's plotting and his characters stay beyond the pages present.
woodrow-wilson-as-i-know-him:
Joseph P. Tumulty, Wilson's White House aide, wrote this personal portrait of President Woodrow Wilson. His preface warns that Wilson disliked being written about. Friends were expected to stay silent while foes talked. Tumulty tells of a 1920 speech in Bethesda that cooled Wilson's manner for days. Wilson never read the speech, Tumulty believes.

Tumulty still wrote the volume from long daily contact. He drew on Wilson's public addresses and on many earlier books. Readers get an insider's view of Wilson's habits, pride, and reserve. Loyalty and candour mix in the telling, since Tumulty knew his subject might never open the volume.
